newsitem.title: USA: Blue chips rise for third day in a row, dollar higher.
newsitem.headline: Blue chips rise for third day in a row, dollar higher.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks Tuesday continued their charge back from last week's rout, lifted by another rally in technology stocks and bargain hunting, while the dollar rose to a 4-1/2-year high against Japan's yen.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell. Gasoline prices rose, partly due to gasoline shortages in oil-producing nations Saudi Arabia and Nigeria, analysts said.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 53.25 points at 6,609.16, having regained more than 130 points from last week's sell-off of 215 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,338 to 1,108 on active volume of 448 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"I think folks are looking at prices, thinking they're reasonably attractive, and stepping up a little bit," said Robert von Pentz, a managing partner at Columbia Partners.
Technology stocks again led the recovery. The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite index rose 6.02 points to 1,257.37, its fourth straight advance.
Analysts said technology stocks, particularily semiconductor makers, got a boost from stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings from Motorola Inc. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.
They also cited positive comments on the sector from Goldman Sachs strategist Abby Joseph Cohen.

In a call to the firm's investors, Cohen said the market correction was over, and the Standard & Poor's 500 stock index was likely to end the year at 850, up from its recent record closing high of 816.29. On Tuesday, the S&P ended at 766.12, up 3.99 points.
"This has been a very dramatic period for the U.S. financial markets, but we remain optimistic about the U.S. market outlook," Cohen said.

"We believe the U.S. economy is nowhere near recession, inflation is under very good control, and we are making no change in our asset allocation. We are comfortable with our year-end price targets," she said.

Stocks moved higher despite a weak Treasury market, where the 30-year bond was off 12/32, or $3.75 on a $1,000 bond, in late trading, sending its yield up to 7.10 percent from Monday's close of 7.07 percent. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.

While stock market trading in the past weeks has been dominated by concern over rising interest rates, first-quarter earnings reports will be the focus of Wall Street in the coming sessions, analysts said.
"From now on it looks like it's going to depend on earnings," said Harry Laubscher, an analyst at Tucker Anthony.

The dollar touched 126.52 Japanese yen, its highest level since August 1992, in European trading after the Jiji news service quoted Japanese Vice Trade Minister Tsutomu Makino as saying the weak yen was more positive than negative for the country's economy at the moment.

The dollar gave up some of those gains in late New York trading but still ended solidly higher at 126.30 yen, up from 125.58 yen Monday. The dollar also rose against Germany's currency, to 1.7155 marks from 1.7125 marks Monday.
In commodity markets, gasoline prices rose on shortages in Saudi Arabia and Nigeria and due to a periodic scheduling deadline at a pipeline terminal in Houston, analysts said.

Gasoline for May delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange settled up 0.45 cent a gallon at 61.17 cents. May heating oil ended off 0.23 cent a gallon at 52.89 cents while May crude finished up 12 cents a barrel at $19.35.
In overseas markets, the London Stock Exchange's FTSE 100 index closed 2.4 points down at 4,269.3. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average rose 306.03 points, or 1.73 percent, ending at 18,021.70.
